title: Dimension of the witness geometry for several recording channels

key_results.statement: For a medium of cells $c_1,\dots,c_m$ in a product state, $C=\sum_h\lvert h\rangle\langle h\rvert\otimes K_h$ with $K_h=\sum_{c=1}^mK^{(c)}_h$ on $\mathcal H_M=\bigotimes_c\mathcal H_c$ is a recording contract of the setting of 05, so (5.10), (5.11), (5.13), (5.14), (10.8) and (10.12) carry over to the whole medium under $\mathcal H_c\to\mathcal H_M$, $d_c\to D$, $K_h\to\sum_cK^{(c)}_h$, $\chi\to\bigotimes_c\chi_c$.

The record vector of the whole medium is $u_h=\sum_{c=1}^m\iota_c\bigl(u^{(c)}_h\bigr)$, where $\iota_c(v)=\lvert\chi_1\rangle\otimes\cdots\otimes v\otimes\cdots\otimes\lvert\chi_m\rangle$ puts $v$ into cell $c$; the images of different channels are mutually orthogonal.

$\langle u_h\vert u_{h'}\rangle=\sum_c\langle u^{(c)}_h\vert u^{(c)}_{h'}\rangle$ and $d_0(h,h')^2=\sum_{c=1}^md^{(c)}_0(h,h')^2$ with $d^{(c)}_0(h,h')=\lVert u^{(c)}_h-u^{(c)}_{h'}\rVert$; hence $h\sim_0h'$ iff $u^{(c)}_h=u^{(c)}_{h'}$ in every channel $c$.

With $V=\{t\in\mathbb R^H:\sum_ht_h=0\}$ and $A_ct=\sum_ht_hu^{(c)}_h$, the read-out space of channel $c$ is $F_c=(\ker A_c)^{\perp}\subset V$, the space of centred functions $h\mapsto g(w,u^{(c)}_h)$ with $w\in\mathcal H_c$; it satisfies $\dim F_c=\dim^{(c)}_0$.
$\dim_0=\dim_{\mathbb R}(F_1+F_2+\cdots+F_m)$: the dimension of the whole witness geometry is the dimension of the sum of the channel read-out spaces.

$\dim_0=\sum_c\dim^{(c)}_0$ iff the sum $F_1+\cdots+F_m$ is direct, i.e. iff $F_c\cap\sum_{c'\neq c}F_{c'}=\{0\}$ for every $c$; in terms of the records the condition reads: if $h\mapsto\sum_cg(w_c,u^{(c)}_h)$ is constant on $H$ for some $w_c\in\mathcal H_c$, then every $h\mapsto g(w_c,u^{(c)}_h)$ is constant.

$\max_c\dim^{(c)}_0\le\dim_0\le\min\bigl(n-1,\sum_c\dim^{(c)}_0\bigr)$ and $\sum_c\dim^{(c)}_0\le2\sum_c(d_c-1)\le2D-2$ with $D=\prod_cd_c$; the lower bound is attained for identical channels (all $F_c$ equal), the upper bound whenever (14.6) holds.

For a closed polygon $h_1,\dots,h_k$ with $k\ge3$ and $h_{k+1}=h_1$, $\Phi(h_1,\dots,h_k;\lambda)=-\lambda^2\sum_{c=1}^m\Omega^{(c)}(h_1,\dots,h_k)+O(\lambda^3)$ with $\Omega^{(c)}=\sum_{j=1}^k\omega\bigl(u^{(c)}_{h_j},u^{(c)}_{h_{j+1}}\bigr)$, so the $\lambda^2$ loop term is a sum of channel contributions.

For one channel, with $\langle X\rangle_c=\langle\chi_c\vert X\vert\chi_c\rangle$ and the channel index of $K$ suppressed, $\langle u^{(c)}_h\vert u^{(c)}_{h'}\rangle=\langle K_hK_{h'}\rangle_c-\langle K_h\rangle_c\langle K_{h'}\rangle_c$ and $\omega\bigl(u^{(c)}_h,u^{(c)}_{h'}\bigr)=\frac{1}{2\mathrm i}\bigl\langle[K_h,K_{h'}]\bigr\rangle_c$.

For a channel with pairwise commuting $K_h=\sum_j\kappa_h(j)P_j$, $p_j=\langle\chi_c\vert P_j\vert\chi_c\rangle$ and $\bar\kappa_h=\sum_jp_j\kappa_h(j)=\langle K_h\rangle_c$: $\langle u^{(c)}_h\vert u^{(c)}_{h'}\rangle=\sum_jp_j\bigl(\kappa_h(j)-\bar\kappa_h\bigr)\bigl(\kappa_{h'}(j)-\bar\kappa_{h'}\bigr)$ and $d^{(c)}_0(h,h')^2=\operatorname{Var}_p(\kappa_h-\kappa_{h'})$, so the Gram matrix is a real symmetric positive semidefinite covariance matrix.

A commuting channel contributes nothing to the $\lambda^2$ term of the loop phases: $\omega\bigl(u^{(c)}_h,u^{(c)}_{h'}\bigr)=0$ for all $h,h'$, hence $\Omega^{(c)}(h_1,\dots,h_k)=0$ for every closed polygon.

For a commuting channel with $S=\{j:p_j>0\}$ and $r_\chi=\lvert S\rvert$, $\dim^{(c)}_0=\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb R}\bigl[\mathbf 1,\ \kappa_h-\kappa_{h_0}\ (h\neq h_0)\bigr]_S-1\le\min(n,r_\chi)-1\le\min(n,d_c)-1$, the matrix having these columns restricted to the rows $j\in S$; the first bound is attained iff the matrix has full rank, and the value $\min(n-1,d_c-1)$ iff in addition $r_\chi=d_c$ (all joint eigenspaces one-dimensional, $\chi_c$ with a nonzero component along every joint eigenvector).

Under S2 (independent draws, absolutely continuous within each channel class), for almost every draw $\dim_0=\min\bigl(n-1,\sum_{c=1}^m\delta_c\bigr)$, with $\delta_c=2(d_c-1)$ for a complex generic channel and $\delta_c=d_c-1$ for a real or commuting channel.
Under S2, the $\lambda^2$ term of $\Phi(h_1,h_2,h_3;\lambda)$ for a triangle of distinct places is generically nonzero iff some channel is complex generic with $d_c\ge2$; otherwise it is zero.

Generically, for $n\ge4$, $\dim_0=3$ iff $\sum_c\delta_c=3$ when $n\ge5$, and iff $\sum_c\delta_c\ge3$ when $n=4$; for $n\ge5$ the solutions are GUE(2)+R(2), R(4), R(3)+R(2) and R(2)+R(2)+R(2) (R: real or commuting channel, $d_c$ in parentheses), and only the first has a generically nonzero $\lambda^2$ loop term.

The smallest total medium dimension $D=\prod_cd_c$ with $\dim_0=3$ is $D_{\min}=4$ both with and without a generically nonzero $\lambda^2$ loop term for $n\ge5$ (GUE(2)+R(2), resp. R(4)); for $n=4$ it is $D_{\min}=3$ with loop data (a single complex generic qutrit) and $D_{\min}=4$ without (R(4)).

Cubic lattice, $h=(x,y,z)\in\{1,\dots,N\}^3$ with $N\ge2$: $u_h=x\lvert100\rangle+y\lvert010\rangle+z\lvert001\rangle$ and $d_0(h,h')=\sqrt{(x-x')^2+(y-y')^2+(z-z')^2}$, so $(H,d_0)$ is isometric to $\{1,\dots,N\}^3\subset\mathbb R^3$ with the Euclidean distance.
Cubic lattice: $\dim_0=3$, and for every lattice triangle $\Phi(h_1,h_2,h_3;\lambda)=O(\lambda^3)$, i.e. the $\lambda^2$ term vanishes.
Plane plus line: $u_h=(x+\mathrm iy)\lvert10\rangle+z\lvert01\rangle$ and $\langle u_h\vert u_{h'}\rangle=xx'+yy'+zz'+\mathrm i\,(xy'-yx')$.

Plane plus line: $d_0(h,h')=\sqrt{(x-x')^2+(y-y')^2+(z-z')^2}$, so $(H,d_0)$ is again isometric to the Euclidean $\{1,\dots,N\}^3\subset\mathbb R^3$, and $\dim_0=3$ with $\dim^{(1)}_0=2$ and $\dim^{(2)}_0=1$.

Plane plus line, lattice triangle $h_j=(x_j,y_j,z_j)$: $\Phi(h_1,h_2,h_3;\lambda)=-\lambda^2\bigl[(x_2-x_1)(y_3-y_1)-(x_3-x_1)(y_2-y_1)\bigr]+O(\lambda^3)$, where the bracket is twice the signed area of the triangle's projection onto the $(x,y)$ coordinates; the $\lambda^2$ term is nonzero iff the projected points are not collinear.

open_issues: The carry-over (Step 1) assumes that the constructions of 05 and 10 refer to the medium only as the companion part of the recorded object a (view and branch states). Only their quoted equations were available.
Two parts of S2 are readings of 'generically within a class': the independence of the channels, and the definition of the generic commuting class.
Only the λ² term of the loop phases is determined. For real and commuting channels the loop phases are O(λ³); higher orders are not addressed.
For n = 4, dim₀ = 3 = n − 1 is the maximal possible value, so the condition (14.15) is then only a threshold.

consistency_checks.check: Scaling: under K → sK with s > 0, u → su and d₀ → s·d₀, so λd₀ is invariant under λ → λ/s; ω → s²ω, so λ²Ω is invariant in (14.8) and (14.21); dim₀, the per-channel dimensions and δ_c are unchanged.

Single channel (m = 1): ι₁ is the identity and (14.2), (14.3) reduce to (5.10); (14.5) gives dim₀ equal to the channel dimension, the two bounds in (14.7) coincide and (14.6) holds trivially; (14.8) reduces to (10.8) and (14.13) reduces to (7.7) and (7.11).

Loop reversal: reversing (h₁, …, hₖ) flips the sign of every Ω^(c) because ω is antisymmetric; in (14.21) exchanging h₂ and h₃ flips the sign of the bracket; cross-check of (14.9) in Step 9: the commutator [x σx + y σy, x' σx + y' σy] = 2i(xy' − yx') σz with ⟨0|σz|0⟩ = 1 reproduces ω = xy' − yx'.
